summary: This memo describes an overall strategy for deploying a Directory Service on the Internet, based on the OSI X.500 Directory Service. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1430 is a plan for building a shared directory on the Internet, based on the X.500 standard. It describes what such a directory would hold, who would manage each part of it, and what had to be built before it could work.

questions: how to build a global directory
subtitle: A roadmap for building a global Internet directory based on the X.500 standard.

tldr.problem: The Internet had no shared way to look up people, to hold the X.509 certificates that secure electronic mail, or to find resources, and the Domain Name System did not cover these needs.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1430 proposes an Internet Directory Service built on the OSI X.500 standard, with a hierarchical tree of entries that each country and organization manages for itself, and names assigned from the top down.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Informational and defines no protocol. It lays out what would have to be built, which working groups were building it, and the security and legal questions that a shared directory raises.

today: RFC 1430 is an Informational memo, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It sets out a strategy rather than a specification, so it defines no protocol of its own.

sections.title: What the Internet Needed a Directory For
sections.content:
The memo opens by listing what the Internet wanted from a directory service. In the short term there was pressure to establish two new services: a white pages lookup of users, and support for X.509 authentication in a range of applications, in particular for Privacy Enhanced Mail.

In the medium term the memo expects many more requirements. These include general resource lookup, for information ranging from committee structures to bibliographic data; support for the management of the Internet infrastructure, with configuration information integrated into the higher level directory; support for applications such as electronic distribution lists, capability information on advanced user agents, and the location of files and archive services; and support for mail handling systems, whether RFC 822 or X.400 based, including routing and information on user agent capabilities.

For the longer term, the memo says more sophisticated uses of X.500 are possible, extending it into a useful and fast yellow pages service.
sections.plainLanguage: The first job was to let people look up other people and to hold the certificates that secure electronic mail. Later on, the directory would also hold information about resources, network configuration and mail routing.

sections.title: The Proposed Solution
sections.content:
The memo notes that the Domain Name System could in principle be used for many of these functions, with appropriate extensions, but suggests that a higher level of directory service is needed. It proposes establishing an Internet Directory Service based on X.500, which provides appropriate functionality for the services envisaged and gives flexibility for future extension. That extension could come from tracking the evolution of the OSI standard, from work specific to the Internet, or from a mixture of both.

The aim is a global and universal directory service that gives Internet users fast access to all kinds of data. The memo says the X.500 Directory Service in this case may range from a simple white pages service, information on people and services, to coupling various existing databases and information repositories in a universal way.

Several different but cooperating X.500 directory service pilots were already taking place on the Internet, and the memo calls these an important base for experimenting with the new service. The final goal of the strategy is to deploy a fully operational directory service on the Internet. Section 9 sets out the relationship with the existing Domain Name System: an Experimental Protocol RFC, RFC 1279, proposes mapping DNS information onto the directory, and the memo says experiments should be conducted in that area.
sections.plainLanguage: The plan is to build the directory on the X.500 standard, because it already does what the Internet needs and can grow later. Existing pilots were the starting point, and the DNS would be mapped onto the directory rather than replaced by it.

sections.title: The X.500 Information Framework
sections.content:
The memo says the most critical aspect of the directory service is establishing an Internet information framework, and that mapping data onto it involves substantial effort, far outweighing the technical effort of building servers and user agents.

The technical model comes from the X.500 standard. It is a hierarchical navigational system that couples distributed databases and lets the organisation or person responsible for the data manage it. Each object in this information structure, called the Directory Information Tree, is represented as an entry. Objects are typed by an object class, which permits multiple inheritance, and an object is described by a set of attributes. Each attribute is typed, attribute types are hierarchical, and each attribute type has an associated attribute syntax, which may be generic or shared with other attributes and may describe something simple such as a string or a bitmap, or something complex with detailed structures. Each entry has an unambiguous and unique global name, and alternate hierarchies can be built with aliases or pointers in distinguished name syntax.

The memo lists possible extensions for the longer term: support of ordered attributes, needed by applications such as message storage; extensions to allow unification with management information associated with SNMP or other management protocols; and handling of non-hierarchical data in a better manner for searching and retrieval while keeping the basic hierarchy for management purposes, which is essentially building a general purpose resource location service on top of the basic infrastructure.

The operational model follows. Larger organisations on the Internet maintain their part of the tree on their own DSA, a Directory System Agent. Smaller organisations rent DSA space from regional networks or other service providers. Together these DSAs form the Internet Directory Service infrastructure, and a special DSA containing the root of the naming hierarchy has to be established and maintained to couple the parts of the tree.
sections.plainLanguage: The directory is a tree. Each entry holds information about one thing and has a name that is unique in the whole tree. The organisation that owns the information looks after its own branch, so a large organisation runs its own part of the tree and a small one rents space.

sections.title: Name Assignment and Delegation
sections.content:
The memo says it is important to define how the naming hierarchy will be structured. Although the basic model suggests a single database with a namespace divided along geographic boundaries, this may not turn out to be the most appropriate model, and different models may evolve according to the needs of the Internet and the applications used on it. Some parts of the tree may be assigned at the root, for example a representation of the domain namespace, and below that several loosely coupled namespaces may exist, each with its own area of applicability.

The core of the tree is nationally assigned, and the parts below country level are managed differently in each country. In many countries registration authorities will be established according to the OSI standard, and in some this has been done by the national ISO member body representative, for example in the UK by BSI. The lower parts of the hierarchy are delegated to organisations that then have control over name assignment in that part of the tree. The memo says there is no reason to mandate how to assign this hierarchy, although it is appropriate to give guidelines.

In North America an alternative approach was being developed by the North American Directory Forum, which leverages existing registration mechanisms. For the Internet, the Internet Society has been suggested as a possible naming authority. The memo asks that the directory service follow evolving national and international hierarchies, but says this should not cause undue delay: the strategy is to proceed with name assignment as needed, establish interim registration authorities where necessary, and take practical steps to be aligned with emerging national authorities wherever possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Each country looks after its own part of the tree and passes names down to the organisations below it. The memo does not force one scheme on everyone. It says to start naming as needed and keep in step with national schemes as they appear.

sections.title: Infrastructure, Rollout and Data Management
sections.content:
Although the technical components of an X.500 infrastructure are clear, the DSAs that hold the data and the DUAs that let users and applications reach it, the memo says a lot more is needed for deployment. Several interim pilots on the Internet had already produced many of the issues: the PSI White Pages Pilot, which was operating as an Internet wide pilot; FOX, a project to explore the development and interoperability of X.500 implementations; and Paradise, which had been providing the glue to hold the various national activities together.

The short term requirements are central operations run as a service for the whole Internet: a root DSA containing the top level of the tree, which at the time was managed by the Paradise project; name assignment; knowledge management, the information on which DSA holds what part of the tree and how it can be reached; and replication of knowledge and data, since for the directory to perform well the information high up in the tree must be significantly replicated. The memo also wants enough implementations to give full coverage over different hardware and software platforms, an executive summary to persuade managers to invest manpower, and user agents tuned intelligently for the applications they serve. To let users reach the service from low powered workstations, a lightweight protocol has to be developed over TCP/IP; two private ones already existed, the Michigan DIXIE protocol and the PSI Directory Assistance Service, and the IETF OSI Directory Services Working Group was working on a standard one called LDAP. The memo also says the use of STD 35, RFC 1006, to allow OSI applications on top of TCP/IP is essential for deployment in the Internet.

The medium term requirements are enhanced performance for real global usage, a schema extended for data such as NIC data and resource location, and support for Internet Message Handling services. The long term requirements are tracking the evolution of X.500 and feeding back into it, interfacing existing relational database management systems into the directory service, and a lightweight protocol for access and system usage to increase performance for wider applications such as policy based routing.

The memo warns that the infrastructure will not stand much chance without proper data management, and because the management of data is distributed over many sources it is impossible to describe one single procedure for it. Guidelines will have to be developed to describe a minimum level of quality, and pilot data management projects will have to connect existing databases to the directory. Section 6.1 notes that most countries have laws that dictate how data on people can and cannot be made available, that these laws differ from country to country, and that each national organisation should research the laws that apply to it. In the meantime a general User Bill of Rights should be established, drafted by the IETF IDS Working Group, using the NADF User Bill of Rights as a basis.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the directory can run, some central jobs are needed: a root for the tree, a way to hand out names, a map of which server holds which part of the tree, and copies of the information near the top so lookups are quick. Each organisation also has to keep its own data tidy and follow the privacy law of its own country.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The memo argues that a directory can be an important component in the overall provision of security in a distributed system, especially where public key cryptography is used. The directory can serve as a repository for authentication information, which forms the basis of OSI authentication services such as X.400 and of non-OSI services such as privacy enhanced mail. It may also use stored authentication information to provide security services for the directory system itself.

Section 8.1 covers the directory's role in authentication. X.509 strong authentication places minimal requirements on the directory, but in practice this kind of authentication can be deployed only on a limited scale without a directory, which makes the provision critical for applications such as Privacy Enhanced Mail. In the framework adopted by PEM, a certification authority applies a digital signature to a collection of data consisting of a user's public component, information that identifies the user, and the identity of the organisation vouching for it. The result is a certificate, and the organisation named is the issuer. Certificates can then be stored in directory servers and sent over unsecured channels, because the signature can be checked without trusting the transport. The memo also says that a security policy is needed, and mentions a read-only system containing only public data as one of the policies a deployment could be based on.

Section 8.2 lists the security services that are possible. They are peer authentication at bind, established during the bind operation between a DUA and a DSA or between two DSAs, using simple passwords, one-way hashed passwords or public key cryptography, though most existing implementations use only simple passwords. Then per-operation authentication and integrity, which identifies the DUA that originated an operation and can verify the DSA that returned data, with integrity ensured by digital signatures. Then single entry access control, which most DSA implementations provide; multiple entry access control, used to control searching so that information and organisational structure cannot be trawled, although it is limited by the need to allow some legitimate browsing for white pages. Then service authorization, which lets DSAs control service in a data independent manner, for example preventing students from making non-local queries while permitting faculty and staff. The memo notes that the directory has no explicit feature to protect the confidentiality of data in transit, and that this is left to lower layer security protocols or local facilities. There is no Internet-wide security policy for directories, and the memo recommends an informational RFC analysing whether global minimum security mechanisms are needed to promote widespread use.
sections.plainLanguage: The directory can hold the certificates that prove who someone is, and it can decide who may read or change which entries. It has no rules of its own for keeping data private while it travels, so that job is left to the network layer.

items.title: Peer authentication at bind
items.text: Identifies the parties when a session is set up.

items.title: Per-operation authentication
items.text: Identifies who asked for a change and who answered a query.

items.title: Single entry access control
items.text: Decides which users may read and change one entry.

items.title: Multiple entry access control
items.text: Limits searching so that the tree cannot be trawled.

items.title: Service authorization
items.text: Allows or refuses a kind of query by the kind of user.

items.title: Security policy
items.text: Sets the goals that the other mechanisms enforce.
